lesson.grammar_point: future continuous (will be + -ing) vs future perfect (will have + past participle) for predictions and deadlines

listenings.text: I have been building AI systems for eight years, so people often ask me to predict the future. Here is my honest view. In five years, most companies will be using AI assistants that read and summarize documents. That part is almost certain. By then, these systems will have learned to write quotes and standard emails in many languages, very well. They will be faster than any human. But there is one thing they will not have learned, in my opinion: to take responsibility. If a machine makes a mistake in a contract, who signs it? Who answers to the client? A person. So my advice to business owners is: use the machine, but keep the signature.

Every time a new technology arrives, people predict the end of work. When spreadsheets appeared in the eighties, everybody said accountants would disappear. Today there are more accountants than ever; they just do different things. I think AI will be similar. By 2035, it will have changed almost every office job, but it won't have eliminated most of them. People will be doing less routine work and more of the things machines are bad at: talking to clients, negotiating, making decisions with incomplete information. And the most valuable skill? Asking good questions, and knowing when the answer is wrong.

When the first AI summaries appeared, I was worried. I thought, in ten years nobody will be reading full books anymore. But something interesting has happened. In our company, readers who use summaries are actually buying more full books, not fewer. The summary works like a trailer. It helps people choose. So I'm optimistic. By the end of this decade, machines will have summarized every book ever written, probably. But a summary will never give you the experience of reading: the voice of the author, the time you spend with the book, the sentence that stays with you for years. That is something you have to do yourself.

paras: Imagine a normal Monday morning in 2030. Before you arrive at the office, an assistant program will have read your emails, summarized the market reports and prepared a list of decisions for the day. While you drink your coffee, a chatbot will be answering your clients’ routine questions. For many companies this is not science fiction: it is the plan for the next five years.

Most experts agree that artificial intelligence will automate a large part of routine office work: reading documents, writing standard emails, preparing quotes. Some jobs will be phased out, and a large part of the workforce will need a new skill set. But the same experts are careful about one thing. Algorithms are fast, but they are not always accurate, and they cannot take responsibility for a decision. The more companies rely on them, the more they will need people who can check what the machine says.

For small and medium companies, the challenge is to keep up with the technology without losing what makes them special: relationships, experience and human judgment. A machine can summarize a book in seconds, but it cannot decide which book will change your life. By 2030, AI will probably have replaced many tasks. It will not have replaced the people who know what to do with the answers.
